    19. Approximate identities and mollification#

    In the notes 18. Convolution, we introduce the convolution product of a function and and proved Young’s inequality . In these notes, we use convolution as a mechanism for approximation in by introducing a sequence of functions of integral and whose mass concentrates at the origin as . Such a family of functions is known as an approximate identity. We will show that if is a sequence of functions that converges in to .

    The reason for this is that the convolution with can be understood as as an average of translates of , If is supported in a small ball around , only translates with close to then enter the average, and by the continuity of translations in (Theorem 14.8) these translates are close to , in the sense of .

    On the other hand, we will see that given that are infinitely differentiable, the derivatives of the convolution can be placed on them, so the approximations of are infinitely differentiable. This yields the density of infinitely differentiable functions in for , which strengthens the density of proved in the notes 14. Dense subclasses of .

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Estimate by an average of with weights .

    • Define approximate identities, and construct a smooth compactly supported approximate identity from a smooth step function and a smooth cutoff.

    • Prove that the mollifications of converge to in for , and explain why this fails for .

    • Justify differentiation under the integral sign by domination, and prove that the derivatives of a mollification fall on the kernel.

    • Determine where the convolution of two functions with bounded support vanishes, and prove that is dense in for .

By Proposition 18.4, the two forms agree wherever either integral converges absolutely. Throughout these notes, unless is stated explicitly. We write for the open ball and for the closed ball of radius centered at .

    19.4 Smoothness of mollifications#

    We now study the regularizing effect of convolution with a smooth compactly supported kernel (Figure 19.4). The mechanism places the derivatives onto the kernel: in , the variable appears only in the smooth factor.

    The value is an average of over the interval , with the weights given by the kernel . The scale separates two kinds of features of (Figure 19.5). Oscillations of that are much shorter than have many periods inside the window, and the average removes them. Variations that are much longer than are nearly constant across the window, and the average keeps them. A jump is spread over an interval of length around it. As , fewer and fewer features of are shorter than ; this is the heuristic behind Theorem 19.7, which turns it into an estimate in .

    A multi-index is a -tuple of integers , of order , and is the partial derivative obtained by differentiating times in the -th coordinate. A function belongs to if exists and is continuous for every multi-index , and to if, in addition, it has compact support. For , .

    Since , Theorem 19.14 contains the density of in for Lebesgue measure, but it does not give an independent proof of it: Theorem 19.7 relies on the continuity of translations, whose proof uses the density of . What it adds is that the approximating functions have derivatives of every order. An identity involving derivatives can therefore be verified first for functions in and then extended to by density.
